description: We are Akshita and Kanishk, a Manchester team on Earth System Trend Detective. Kanishk (MSc AI, University of Manchester) builds AI and web apps; Akshita (Actuarial Science and Maths) leads the statistics and the pitch. Together we won QuantiHack 2026 and placed 3rd at the AMD Developer Hackathon. We are building a website that shows whether an Earth variable is really changing, how fast and where. Our team is complete, but we’re happy to chat with other teams!
summary:
Trend Detective lets anyone pick a place on Earth and a NASA variable (temperature, rain, soil moisture, haze, greenness and more) and find out whether it's really changing or whether it could just be chance.

That question matters because quick trend analyses over-claim. Across 111 places and 19 NASA variables, 29% of the trends a typical test calls real don't hold up once month-to-month noise is handled properly.

So we test each trend properly, then try to explain it away. Could a change of satellite have caused it? Is it El Niño? Does one year carry it? Then we call witnesses: station thermometers, rain gauges and the GRACE satellites that weigh water, each labelled for how independent it really is.

A world globe runs the same test on 4,498 land squares, with a luck test: on shuffled records, a typical test still finds trends 22% of the time, ours 7%. An "around 2050" view puts each trend next to climate models and three emission paths.

People decide things about water, farming and heat based on claims like these. We show which ones NASA's data actually supports, and link every number back to its source.
details:
CODE AND DEMO

GitHub (code, 30-second video, slides, notebook): https://github.com/romaaurora787/trend-detective

Live demo: https://kaakserver.tail042e87.ts.net/trend-detective/

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

You pick a place anywhere on Earth and a NASA variable: temperature, rain, soil moisture, cloud, haze, greenness and more. Or you start from one of our demo cases (Lincolnshire, Delhi, Central Wisconsin, Luzon). The site then goes through the evidence in order.

First, the test. You see the raw monthly record, then the same record with the seasons taken out, then the rate of change (Sen's slope, with a 95% range). Then the question that matters: could this be chance? We answer it with a Mann-Kendall test corrected for month-to-month persistence (Hamed-Rao). One warm month tends to follow another, and ordinary tests count that as extra evidence when it isn't. The verdict is one of four: strong evidence, some evidence, not yet (with roughly how many more years it would take), or no meaningful trend.

Next, the cross-examination, where we try to explain the trend away. Could a change of satellite or data source have caused it? NASA POWER switched its sunlight and cloud data to CERES in 2001, for example. Is it El Niño? We remove El Niño, the NAO, the Indian Ocean Dipole and the PDO together. Does a single year carry the whole trend? Is it really one sudden jump?

Then the witnesses: other records for the same place. NASA's GISTEMP station thermometers, NOAA weather stations, NASA GPCP and IMERG rainfall, ESA CCI soil moisture, NASA GLDAS, the GRACE satellites that weigh stored water, and ERA5. Each says how independent it is of NASA's main record, because two records built from the same inputs agreeing doesn't prove much.

Around that sit a report card of every variable for a place, maps corrected for false discoveries, a two-place comparison and a world globe of 4,498 land squares. There's also an "around 2050" view: the proven trend extended, next to 7 CMIP6 climate models and 3 IPCC emission paths. It isn't a forecast, and if the change was one sudden jump it won't draw a straight line at all.

BENEFITS

Quick trend analyses over-claim, and we can put a number on it. Across 111 places and 19 NASA variables, 29% of the trends a typical test calls real don't survive once the noise is handled properly. We tried our method on thousands of simulated records where we knew the answer. A typical test raised false alarms 28-55% of the time; ours 6-7%, and ours still caught 99.7% of real trends of 0.3 per decade. Every verdict also says what could overturn it and how long until we'd know. A Plain/Detailed switch keeps the test names and p-values out of the way unless you want them.

INTENDED IMPACT

People make real decisions on claims like "rain is falling here" or "this town is warming fast": students, teachers, journalists, farmers, councils. We want any of them to be able to ask NASA's data "is it really changing?" and get an honest answer, including "we can't tell yet". Every number can be checked. Each case links to the exact NASA request, the same box in NASA Giovanni, a CSV, and a notebook that rebuilds the headline result from NASA's public API alone.

TOOLS

Python (FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, pymannkendall, rasterio, xarray), TypeScript and React (Vite, d3-geo, Leaflet), Docker, Git/GitHub and Jupyter. Data from NASA POWER (MERRA-2, CERES), MODIS, GPM IMERG, GPCP, GISTEMP, GLDAS, GRACE/GRACE-FO and Blue Marble, plus ESA CCI, ERA5, the Met Office and NOAA. No special hardware.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

We treat each trend as a suspect, and the case page reads like a trial: evidence, cross-examination, witnesses, verdict.

Our own data fooled us once. At 42 of the 88 places where cloud cover looked like it was changing, one jump at the 2001 satellite switch explained the data better than a steady trend. So we built that check into the tool, and it now runs on every variable with a documented data switch.

The globe has a "luck test". Shuffle each square's years so no trend can exist, then run the tests again. A typical test still finds trends in 22% of squares. Ours finds them in 7%.

When the records disagree, we say so. In Delhi, NASA's model shows no proven warming, while NASA's own station thermometers show +0.21 °C per decade.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Getting the statistics right came first: persistence from month to month, testing thousands of places at once, instruments changing mid-record, and whether a second record is really independent. After that, plain words for people who aren't statisticians, with the detail one click away. Open data and open code, with citations ready to copy. Every verdict number is computed from the data by code; none is written by AI. The site works on a phone, copes when NASA's servers are busy, and credits every data source and licence.
